subject.title: ("O make me a mask and a wall...")
subject.author: Dylan Thomas
subject.text:
u
O make me a mask and a wall to shut from your spies
Of the sharp, enamelled eyes and the spectacled claws
Rape and rebellion in the nurseries of my face,
Gag of a dumbstruck tree to block from bare enemies
The bayonet tongue in this undefended prayerpiece,
The present mouth, and the sweetly blown trumpet of lies,
Shaped in old armor and oak the countenance of a dunce
To shield the glistening brain and blunt the examiners,
And a tear-stained widower grief drooped from the lashes
To veil belladonna and let the dry eyes perceive
Others betray the lamenting lies of their losses
By the curve of the nude mouth or the laugh up the sleeve.

                      ur
   Not from this anger, anticlimax after
   Refusal struck her loins and the lame flower
   Bent like a beast to lap the singular floods
   In a land without weather,
   Shall she receive a bellyfull of weeds
   And bear those tendril hands I touch across
   The agonised, two seas.

    Behind my head a square of sky sags over
   The circular smile tossed from lover to lover

title: The Poem Above You Is Actually Two
standfirst: What the sheet renders as one continuous poem is, on the page it comes from, two separate Dylan Thomas poems fused by a scrape that swallowed the numerals between them. They ran together once, in Chicago in August 1938, and Thomas split them apart himself within the year.

sections.heading: Two Poems Filed as One
sections.body:
Above this piece the sheet carries two stray marks where headings should be: a lone `u` before the first stanza, and `ur` nine lines later. They read as scanning noise, and that is close to what they are — but noise from something specific. The text beginning "O make me a mask and a wall" and the text beginning "Not from this anger, anticlimax after" are not two stanzas of one poem. They are two separate Dylan Thomas poems, run together here because whatever separated them on the printed page — almost certainly the roman numerals I and II — survived the trip into this file as two orphaned lower-case fragments and nothing else.

Read past the point where most readers stop:

> Others betray the lamenting lies of their losses
> By the curve of the nude mouth or the laugh up the sleeve.

That couplet ends the poem most people mean when they say "O Make Me a Mask." Everything after the `ur` belongs to a different poem, written for a different occasion, and it has spent most of its life being read by almost no one.

sections.heading: Chicago, August 1938
sections.body: Both poems ran on the same page of *Poetry*, in Chicago, in August 1938 — Thomas was twenty-three. The same issue carried a third Thomas poem, "When All My Five and Country Senses See," so this was not one submission slipping through but a small cluster of his work landing in an American magazine at once. [Harriet Monroe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harriet_Monroe), who had built the magazine from nothing in 1912, had been dead not quite two years by then, felled by a stroke on a trip to Peru in September 1936. The man reading Thomas's pages in 1938 was [George Dillon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Dillon_%28poet%29), in the first full year of his own editorship. It was Dillon's magazine, not Monroe's, that put a self-concealing sonnet and an angrier poem about a woman's refusal back to back on one page — a pairing that lasted exactly one printing.

sections.heading: One Kept, One Let Go
sections.body: A year after Chicago, Thomas gathered both poems into [The Map of Love](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_works_by_Dylan_Thomas), his third collection, published by Dent in 1939. This time they stand apart — separate entries, no numbers linking them, no shared page. From there their fortunes diverge hard. "O Make Me a Mask and a Wall" became one of the most anthologized twelve lines Thomas wrote: tight, self-contained, quotable entire, the poem most readers meet first. ["Not From This Anger"](https://allpoetry.com/poem/8451761-Not-From-This-Anger-by-Dylan-Thomas) did not; it survives mainly in complete-poems reprints and specialist reading sites, rarely excerpted, rarely discussed on its own. Whatever made the two of them a pair on one page in Chicago did not survive contact with a book Thomas assembled and ordered himself.

sections.heading: What Changed on the Way to the Book
sections.body: The text preserved on the page above is not identical to the poems as they are usually printed now, in either half. Poetry set "old armor and oak" in 1938; the same line in ["O Make Me a Mask"](https://www.poemhunter.com/poem/o-make-me-a-mask/), as anthologized today, runs "old armour and oak" — the magazine's American spelling never carried over into the British book. In "Not From This Anger," the 1938 text has "her loins," plural, and "In a land without weather"; the version usually quoted now has ["her loin"](https://allpoetry.com/poem/8451761-Not-From-This-Anger-by-Dylan-Thomas), singular, and "In a land strapped by hunger" — a vague geography swapped for a specific deprivation. Nothing in what I could find explains either change; Thomas revised obsessively and rarely left notes on why. But it means the poem above is not simply an old copy of a fixed text — it is one specific, dated draft of a poem Thomas kept rewriting after it left his hands.

sections.heading: A Draft Five Years Older Than the Magazine
sections.body: "O Make Me a Mask" has a longer paper trail than one issue of *Poetry* suggests. By one detailed reading of Thomas's surviving notebooks, an early version sits in the third notebook as poem number eighteen, dated March 1933 — Thomas was eighteen, still living in Swansea, five years and an ocean from the Chicago printing above. He returned to it in [November 1937](https://ramblingatthebridgehead.wordpress.com/2018/02/27/o-make-me-a-mask-by-dylan-thomas/), four months after marrying Caitlin Macnamara, and cut it down hard into something close to the twelve lines printed here. What was lost from the 1933 draft, or why that particular month prompted the rewrite, is not part of the record I could find. What is clear is that a poem which now reads as one confident, unbroken gesture took the better part of five years, one marriage, and at least one serious act of cutting to arrive at the version anyone quotes.
